9. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
9. Ex parte enim cognoscimus, et ex parte prophetamus:
10. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
10. At ubi venerit quod perfectum est, tunc, quod ex parte est, abolebitur.
11. When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
11. Quum essem puer, ut puer loquebar, ut puer sentiebam, ut puer cogitabam: at postquam factus sum vir, abolevi puerilia.
12. For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
12. Cernimus enim nunc per speculum in aenigmate: tunc autem facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte: tune vero cognoscam, quem admodum et cognitus sum.
13. And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
13. Nunc autem manet fides, spes, caritas, tria haec: sed maxima ex his est caritas.
entries.4e7aca3d01cc5280aaf9cc47d3c46bdda1e05c80: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.13.9" sID="gen119565" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119566" type="x-p"/>He now proves that <hi type="italic">prophecy, </hi>and other gifts of that nature, are done away, <note n="798"> <div sID="gen119567" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Seront un iour abolis</foreign>;” — “Will one day be done away.”<div eID="gen119567" type="x-p"/> </note> because they are conferred upon us to help our infirmity. Now our imperfection will one day have an end. Hence the use, even of those gifts, will, at the same time, be discontinued, for it were absurd that they should remain and be of no use. They will, therefore, perish. This subject he pursues to the end of the chapter.<div eID="gen119566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">We know in part</hi> This passage is misinterpreted by most persons, as if it meant that our knowledge, and in like manner our prophecy, is not yet perfect, but that we are daily making progress in them. Paul’s meaning, however, is — that it is owing to our imperfection that we at present have knowledge and prophecy. Hence the phrase <hi type="italic">in part</hi> means — “Because we are not yet perfect.” Knowledge and prophecy, therefore, have place among us so long as that imperfection cleaves to us, to which they are helps. It is true, indeed, that we ought to make progress during our whole life, and that everything that we have is merely begun. Let us observe, however, what Paul designs to prove — that the gifts in question are but temporary. Now he proves this from the circumstance, that the advantage of them is only for a time — so long as we aim at the mark by making progress every day.<div eID="gen119568" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119565" osisID="1Cor.13.9" type="section"/>
entries.c5a528d1eb61703c06b5ee76df0a553055b945bb: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.13.10" sID="gen119569" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">When that which is perfect is come</hi> “When the goal has been reached, then the helps in the race will be done away.” He retains, however, the form of expression that he had already made use of, when he contrasts <hi type="italic">perfection</hi> with what is <hi type="italic">in part</hi> “Perfection,” says he, “when it will arrive, will put an end to everything that aids imperfection.” But when will that perfection come? It begins, indeed, at death, for then we put off, along with the body, many infirmities; but it will not be completely manifested until the day of judgment, as we shall hear presently. Hence we infer, that the whole of this discussion is ignorantly applied to the time that is intermediate.<div eID="gen119570" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119569" osisID="1Cor.13.10" type="section"/>
entries.4f5f796a699ce3fa5209e8025ae7bb30ae2fb2a5: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.13.11" sID="gen119571" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">When I was a child</hi> He illustrates what he had said, by a similitude. For there are many things that are suitable to children, which are afterwards done away on arriving at maturity. For example, education is necessary for childhood; it does not comport with mature age. <note n="799"> <div sID="gen119573" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Elle ne conuient point a ceux qui sont en aage de discretion</foreign>;” — “It does not become those who are at the age of discretion?’<div eID="gen119573" type="x-p"/> </note> So long as we live in this world, we require, in some sense, education. We are far from having attained, as yet, the perfection of wisdom. That perfection, therefore, which will be in a manner a maturity of spiritual age, will put an end to education and its accompaniments. In his Epistle to the Ephesians, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.14">Ephesians 4:14</reference>,) he exhorts us to be no <hi type="italic">longer children; </hi>but he has there another consideration in view, of which we shall speak when we come to that passage.<div eID="gen119572" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119571" osisID="1Cor.13.11" type="section"/>
entries.a52af8a5f32af6e7dbc9888af8c1996ebf2aa8c4: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Cor.13.12" sID="gen119574" type="section"/> <div sID="gen119575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">We now see through a glass</hi> Here we have the application of the similitude. “The measure of knowledge, that we now have, is suitable to imperfection and childhood, as it were; for we do not as yet see clearly the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom, and we do not as yet enjoy a distinct view of them.” To express this, he makes use of another similitude — that <hi type="italic">we now see only as in a glass, </hi>and therefore but obscurely. This obscurity he expresses by the term <hi type="italic">enigma</hi> <note n="800"> <div sID="gen119576" type="x-p"/> The original term <foreign xml:lang="el">αἴνιγμα</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">enigma</hi>,) properly means, a <hi type="italic">dark saying</hi> It is employed by classical writers in this sense. See Pind. Fr. 165. Aeseh. <reference osisRef="Bible:Prov.610">Pr. 610</reference>. The Apostle is generally supposed to have had in his eye <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.12.8">Numbers 12:8</reference>, which is rendered in the Septuagint as follows: <foreign xml:lang="el">Στόμα κατὰ στόμα λαλήσω αὐτῶ ἐν ἔιδει, καὶ οὐ δι ᾿ αἰνίγματων</foreign>; — “I will speak to him mouth to mouth in a vision, and not by <hi type="italic">dark sayings</hi>.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen119576" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen119575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119577" type="x-p"/>In the first place, there can be no doubt that it is the ministry of the word, and the means that are required for the exercise of it, that he compares to a <hi type="italic">looking-glass</hi> For God, who is otherwise invisible, has appointed these means for discovering himself to us. At the same time, this may also be viewed as extending to the entire structure of the world, in which the glory of God shines forth to our view, in accordance with what is stated in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.16">Romans 1:16</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.3.18">2 Corinthians 3:18</reference>. In <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.20">Romans 1:20</reference> the Apostle speaks of the creatures as <hi type="italic">mirrors,</hi> <note n="801"> <div sID="gen119578" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et l’Apostre, en l’onzieme aux Heb., d. 13, nomme les creatures, miroirs</foreign>;” — “And the Apostle, in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.13">Hebrews 11:13</reference>, speaks of the creatures as mirrors.” There is obviously a mistake here in the quotation. Most probably Calvin had in his eye <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.3">Hebrews 11:3</reference>, as a passage similar <hi type="italic">in</hi> <hi type="italic">substance </hi>to <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.20">Romans 1:20</reference>, quoted by him in his Latin Commentary. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen119578" type="x-p"/> </note> in which God’s invisible majesty is to be seen; but as he treats here particularly of spiritual gifts, which are subservient to the ministry of the Church, and are its accompaniments, we shall not wander away from our present subject.<div eID="gen119577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119579" type="x-p"/>The ministry of the word, I say, is like a <hi type="italic">looking-glass</hi> For the angels have no need of preaching, or other inferior helps, nor of sacraments, for they enjoy a vision of God of another kind; <note n="802"> <div sID="gen119580" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ils ont vn autre iouissance de la presence de Dieu</foreign>;” — “They have another enjoyment of the presence of God.”<div eID="gen119580" type="x-p"/> </note> and God does not give them a view of his face merely in a mirror, but openly manifests himself as present with them. We, who have not as yet reached that great height, behold the image of God as it is presented before us in the word, in the sacraments, and, in fine, in the whole of the service of the Church. This vision Paul here speaks of as partaking of obscurity — not as though it were doubtful or delusive, but because it is not so distinct as that which will be at last afforded on the final day. He teaches the same thing in other words, in the <hi type="italic">second </hi>Epistle — (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.7">2 Corinthians 5:7</reference>) — that,<div eID="gen119579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119581" type="x-p"/>so long as we dwell in the body we are absent from the Lord; <lb/> for we walk by faith, not by sight.<div eID="gen119581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119582" type="x-p"/>Our faith, therefore, at present beholds God as absent. How so? Because it sees not his face, but rests satisfied with the image in the <hi type="italic">mirror; </hi>but when we shall have left the world, and gone to him, it will behold him as near and before its eyes.<div eID="gen119582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119583" type="x-p"/>Hence we must understand it in this manner — that the knowledge of God, which we now have from his word, is indeed certain and true, and has nothing in it that is confused, or perplexed, or dark, but is spoken of as comparatively <hi type="italic">obscure, </hi>because it comes far short of that clear manifestation to which we look forward; for then <hi type="italic">we shall see face to face</hi> <note n="803"> <div sID="gen119584" type="x-p"/> “The blessed God’s manifestation of himself,” say’s Mr. Howe, “is emphatically expressed in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.13.12">1 Corinthians 13:12</reference> — of <hi type="italic">seeing face to face</hi>, which signifies on <hi type="italic">his </hi>part, gracious vouchsafement, — his offering his blessed face to view, — that he hides it not, nor turns it away, as here sometimes he doth, in just displeasure. And his face means, even his most conspicuous glory, such as, in this state of mortality, it would be mortal to us to behold; for ‘no man,’ not so divine a man as Moses himself, ‘could see his face and live.’ And it signifies, on <hi type="italic">their </hi>part who are thus made perfect, their applying and turning their face towards his, viz., that they see not casually, or by fortuitous glances, but eye to eye, by direct and most voluntary intuition; which, therefore, on their part, implies moral perfection, the will directing and commanding the eye, and upon inexpressible relishes of joy and pleasure, forbidding its diversion, holds it steady and intent.” Howe’s Works, (Lond. 1834,) p. 1016. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen119584" type="x-p"/> </note> Thus this passage is not at all at variance with other passages, which speak of the clearness, at one time, of the law, at another time, of the entire Scripture, but more especially of the gospel. For we have in the word (in so far as is expedient for us) a naked and open revelation of God, and it has nothing intricate in it, to hold us in suspense, as wicked persons imagine; <note n="804"> <div sID="gen119585" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme imaginent les moqueurs et gens profanes</foreign>;” — “As scoffers and profane persons imagine.”<div eID="gen119585" type="x-p"/> </note> but how small a proportion does this bear to <hi type="italic">that </hi>vision, which we have in our eye! Hence it is only in a comparative sense, that it is termed <hi type="italic">obscure.</hi><div eID="gen119583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119586" type="x-p"/>The adverb <hi type="italic">then </hi>denotes the last day, rather than the time that is immediately subsequent to death. At the same time, although full vision will be deferred until the day of Christ, a nearer view of God will begin to be enjoyed immediately after death, when our souls, set free from the body, will have no more need of the outward ministry, or other inferior helps. Paul, however, as I noticed a little ago, does not enter into any close discussion as to the state of the dead, because the knowledge of that is not particularly serviceable to piety.<div eID="gen119586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119587" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Now I know in part</hi> That is, the measure of our present knowledge is <hi type="italic">imperfect, </hi>as John says in his Epistle, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.3.1 Bible:1John.3.2">1 John 3:1,2</reference>,) that<div eID="gen119587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119588" type="x-p"/>we know, indeed, that we are the sons of God, <lb/> but that it doth not yet appear, until we shall see God as he is.<div eID="gen119588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen119589" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Then</hi> we shall see God — not in his image, but in himself, so that there will be, in a manner, a mutual view.<div eID="gen119589" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Cor.13.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen119574" osisID="1Cor.13.12" type="section"/>

13. But now remaineth faith, hope, love. This is a conclusion from what goes before — that love is more excellent than other gifts; but in place of the enumeration of gifts that he had previously made, he now puts faith and hope along with love, as all those gifts are comprehended under this summary. For what is the object of the entire ministry, but that we may be instructed as to these things?
“En ces trois choses;” — “In these three things.”
Hence the term faith has a larger acceptation here, than in previous instances; for it is as though he had said — “There are, it is true, many and various gifts, but they all point to this object, and have an eye to it.”
To remain, then, conveys the idea, that, as in the reckoning up of an account, when everything has been deducted, this is the sum that remains For faith does not remain after death, inasmuch as the Apostle elsewhere contrasts it with sight, (2 Corinthians 5:7,) and declares that it remains only so long as we are absent from the Lord We are now in possession of what is meant by faith in this passage — that knowledge of God and of the divine will, which we obtain by the ministry of the Church; or, if you prefer it, faith universal, and taken in its proper acceptation. Hope is nothing else than perseverance in faith For when we have once believed the word of God, it remains that we persevere until the accomplishment of these things. Hence, as faith is the mother of hope, so it is kept up by it, so as not to give way.
The greatest of these is love. It is so, if we estimate its excellence by the effects which he has previously enumerated; and farther, if we take into view its perpetuity. For every one derives advantage from his own faith and hope, but love extends its benefits to others. Faith and hope belong to a state of imperfection: love will remain even in a state of perfection. For if we single out the particular effects of faith, and compare them, faith will be found to be in many respects superior. Nay, even love itself, according to the testimony of the same Apostle, (1 Thessalonians 1:3,) is an effect of faith Now the effect is, undoubtedly, inferior to its cause.
Besides, there is bestowed upon faith a signal commendation, which does not apply to love, when John declares that it is our victory, which overcometh the world. (1 John 5:4.) In fine, it is by faith that we are born against that we become the sons of God — that we obtain eternal life, and that Christ dwells in us. (Ephesians 3:17.) Innumerable other things I pass over; but these few are sufficient to prove what I have in view — that faith is, in many of its effects, superior to love. Hence it is evident, that it is declared here to be superior — not in every respect, but inasmuch as it will be perpetual, and holds at present the first place in the preservation of the Church.
It is, however, surprising how much pleasure Papists take in thundering forth these words. “If faith justifies,” say they, “then much more does love, which is declared to be greater.” A solution of this objection is already furnished from what I have stated, but let us grant that love is in every respect superior; what sort of reasoning is that — that because it is greater, therefore it is of more avail for justifying men! Then a king will plow the ground better than a husbandman, and he will make a shoe better than a shoemaker, because he is more noble than either! Then a man will run faster than a horse, and will carry a heavier burden than an elephant, because he is superior in dignity! Then angels will give light to the earth better than the sun and moon, because they are more excellent! If the power of justifying depended on the dignity or merit of faith they might perhaps be listened to; but we do not teach that faith justifies, on the ground of its having more worthiness, or occupying a higher station of honor, but because it receives the righteousness which is freely offered in the gospel. Greatness or dignity has nothing to do with this. Hence this passage gives Papists no more help, than if the Apostle had given the preference to faith above everything else.
CHAPTER 14
1 Corinthians 14:1-6
1. Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.
1. Sectamini caritatem: aemulamini spiritualia, magis autem ut prophetetis.
2. For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries.
2. Nam qui loquitur lingua, non hominibus loquitur sed Deo: nullus enim audit; Spiritu vero loquitur mysteria.
3. But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
3. Caeterum qui prophetat, heminibus loquitur ad aedificationem, exhortationem, et consolationem.
4. He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church.
4. Qui loquitur lingua, se ipsum aedificat; at qui prophetat, Ecclesiam aedificat.
5. I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied: for greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying.
5. Volo autem omnes vos loqui linguis, magis tamen ut prophetetis; maior enim qui prophetat, quam qui linguis loquitur; nisi interpretetur, ut Ecclesia aedificationem accipiat.
6. Now, brethren, if I come unto you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you, except I shall speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine?
6. Nunc autem, fratres, si venero ad vos linguis loquens, quil vobis prodero, nisi vobis loquar aut per revelationem, aut per scientiam, aut per prophetiam, aut per doctrinam?

               <ns0:head>CHAP. XIII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 THough I speak with the tongues of men and of angels <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle had promised in the close of the former Chapter, to shew them a <ns0:hi>more excellent thing</ns0:hi> than Gifts, or a more excellent course, than that they were so hotly pursuing, in their emulation of the <ns0:hi>best Gifts</ns0:hi>; he now cometh to shew them that way, that course: the way was that of <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> the course was the study and pursuing methods how to shew their Love to God, and to one another; for (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>though I speak,</ns0:hi> that is, if I could speak, or admit I did speak, with the Tongues used in all the Nations of the World, and with the <ns0:hi>Tongues of Angels</ns0:hi>; by which some understand the best and most excellent ways of expressing our selves. Angels have no tongues, nor make any articulate audible sounds, by which they understand one another; but yet there is certainly a Society, or intercourse among Angels, which could not be upheld with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out some way amongst them, to communicate their minds and wills each to other. How this is we cannot tell: some of the Schoolmen say, it is by way of <ns0:hi>Impression</ns0:hi>; that way God indeed communicates his Mind sometimes to his people, making se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cret impressions of his Will upon their minds and understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings; but whether Angels can do the like, or what their way is of communicating their minds each to other, is a great Secret, and we ought to be willingly ignorant of what God hath not pleased, in any part of his revealed Will, to tell us. Neither do I judge it a question proper to this place, where the <ns0:hi>Tongues of Angels</ns0:hi> unquestionably signifie the best and most excellent ways of expressing and communicating our selves to others, as <ns0:hi>Manna</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>Angels food, Psal.</ns0:hi> 78.25. that is, the most ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellent food; for <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> being spiritual Substances, need no food, have no mouths to eat, nor bellies to fill, and this the Apostle meaneth. Though I could express my self, or com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />municate my mind to others in the most excellent way, or in the greatest variety of expression, yet if I have not (<ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which we translate) <ns0:hi>Charity,</ns0:hi> but possibly might be better transla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> because we usually by <ns0:hi>Charity</ns0:hi> (in common speech) un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand that indication of brotherly Love, which is in acts of bounty, <ns0:hi>feeding the hungry, cloathing the naked,</ns0:hi> giving to those that are in want, which it is possible that men may do out of meer humanity, or a superstitious opinion of meriting thereby, without any true root of love to our Neighbours; which is ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver true, if it doth not grow out of a Love to God.</ns0:note>, and have not charity <ns0:hi>b,</ns0:hi> I am become <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">If I want <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) a true root of love to men, flow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing from a true Love to God, and out of obedience to his Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept, I am but as <ns0:hi>sounding brass,</ns0:hi> &c. that is, I only make a noise, but it will conduce nothing to my Salvation, it will be of no use to me: But if I have this true root of Love, then it will be of avail to me. And thus the Apostle proveth, that the habit of <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> to God and man in the heart, is far more excellent than the gift of Tongues, which many of the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> had, or co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veted, or boasted in, despising those who had it not.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And though I have <ns0:hi>the gift</ns0:hi> of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12.8, 9, 10. See Matt. 7.22.</ns0:note> prophecy <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It hath been before shewed, that the <ns0:hi>Gift of Prophecy</ns0:hi> sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifieth an extraordinary power or faculty, by which men in those Primitive Times were inabled to reveal the Mind and Will of God, either as to future contingencies, or things which should afterwards come to pass in the World, or by further explication or application of the Mind and Will of God already revealed in holy Writ.</ns0:note>, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Though, saith the Apostle, I had a vast knowledge, and could in any notion comprehend the most sublime and hidden things, whether Divine, or humane:</ns0:note>, and though I have all faith, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 17.6.</ns0:note> so that I could re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />move mountains <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">And though I had all Faith (except that which is saving and justify<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing): he further opens what Faith he meant, <ns0:hi>viz. Faith</ns0:hi> of Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />racles, a firm perswasion, that God would upon my prayer work things beyond the power, and contrary to the course of Nature, (the Apostle alludeth to the words of our Saviour, <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 17.20) yet, saith he, if I have not <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> that true Love to God and men, by which that Faith, which is profitable to Salvation, worketh and sheweth it self:</ns0:note>, and have not charity, I am no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">it will all signifie nothing, be of no profit nor avail unto me in order to my eter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal Salvation. I may perish for ever notwithstanding such gifts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Apostle proceedeth from common gifts, powers, and habits, to actions, and instanceth in two; the first of which might be a great service to men; the latter, an appearance of a great service to God. Though, saith he, I feed the poor with my goods, and that not sparingly, but liberally, so as I spend all my Estate in that way, and make my self as poor as they.</ns0:note>, and though I give my body to be burned <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Though I die in the Cause of Christ, for the Testi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mony of his Gospel, or for owning of his Ways, and that by the sharpest and most cruel <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ort of death, <ns0:hi>burning,</ns0:hi> and be not dragged to the stake, but freely give up my self to that cruel kind of death.</ns0:note>, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Yet if I have not a root and Principle of Love to God in my heart, that carrieth me out to these actions and these sufferings, they all will signifie nothing to me, as to my eternal Salvation and Happiness. From whence we may ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve, That, 1. The highest acts of beneficence or bounty to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards men, (which we usually call good Works) are not meri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />torious at the hand of God, and may be separated from a true root of saving Grace in the Soul. 2. That the greatest suffer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings for and in the Cause of Religion, may be separated from a true root and Principle of saving Grace. 3. That no actions, no sufferings, are sufficient to intitle any Soul to Heaven, further than they proceed from a Principle of true Love to God, and a desire to obey and to please him in what we do. <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> must be the roots and Principles of all those works which are truly good, and acceptable to God, and which will be of any profit or avail to us with reference to our eternal happiness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:453" />4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 10.12. 1 Pet. 4.8.</ns0:note> Charity suffereth long <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Lest the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> shou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>d say to the Apostle, What is this Love you discourse of? Or how shall we know if we have it? The Apostle here gives thirteen notes of a charitable person. By <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Charity</ns0:hi> he either meaneth a charitable person, a Soul possessed of that love, which he had been commending: Or if we take the term plainly, to signifie the <ns0:hi>habit</ns0:hi> it self; the meaning is, it is an habit or power in the Soul, inabling and inclining it to do these things: To <ns0:hi>suffer long,</ns0:hi> not to be too quick and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eachy with brethren that may offend or displease us; the charitable man will withhold and restrain his wrath, not be rash in the expressions of it, and hasty to revenge.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> is kind <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">And <ns0:hi>is kind,</ns0:hi> it disposeth a man to desire to deserve well of all, and to do good to all, as he hath occasion and opportunity, so as it is impossible there should be in a man any thing more oppo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />site to this Grace, than a currish, churlish temper, with a study and desire to do others mischief.</ns0:note>: charity envieth not <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Though a charitable per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son seeth others in an higher and more prosperous condition than himself, yet it doth not trouble him, but he is glad at the preferment, good, and prosperity of other men, however it fareth with himself. Every envious man, that is displeased and angry at anothers <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>aring well, is an uncharitable man, there is no true root of Love to God or to his Neighbour in his heart.</ns0:note>, charity <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>is rash.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> vaunteth not it self <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He doth not prefer himself before others, ambitiously glorying or boasting, and acting rashly to promote his own glory, and sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tisfie his own intemperate desires or lusts.</ns0:note>, is not puffed up <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He is not puffed up, proudly lifting up himself above others, and swelling with high conceits of himself.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Doth not behave it self unseemly <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He doth not behave himself towards any in an uncomely or unbeseeming manner, and will do nothing towards his bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, which in the opinion of men shall be a filthy or indecent action.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 10.24. Phil. 2.4.</ns0:note> seeketh not her own <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">He doth not seek what is his own, that is, what is for his own profit or advantage only; he hath an eye to the good, and advantage of his brother, as well as his own profit and advantage.</ns0:note>, is not easily provoked <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Such a man is not <ns0:hi>easily provoked</ns0:hi>; he is not without his passions, but he is not governed by his passions, and over-ruled by them to fly out extravagantly against his brother upon every light and trivial occasion; he knows how to bear in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />juries, and is willing rather to bear lesser wrongs, losses, and injuries, than to do any thing in revenge of himself, or to the more remarkable prejudice of his neighbour.</ns0:note>, thinketh no evil <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He thinketh <ns0:hi>no evil,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>no mischief,</ns0:hi> nothing that may be hurtful and prejudicial to his neighbour. Or else, he doth not rashly su<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect his neighbour for doing evil, (which possibly may be the better interpretation); and so it teacheth us, That lightly to take up evil reports of our neighbours, is a violation of Charity; for the man that hath a true love to his brother, though he may believe evil of his brother, and charge him with evil, when it evidently appears to him that he is guilty; yet before that be evident to him, he will not suspect, nor think any such things of him.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 10.3. Rom. 1.32.</ns0:note> Rejoyceth not in iniquity <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">He doth not rejoyce in the sinful falls of others.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Joh. 4.</ns0:note> rejoyceth <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>with the truth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in the truth <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">But he rejoyceth in all truth, and the success and prospering of truth in the World, or in the manifestation of any persons truth, or innocency, and righteousness.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Beareth all things <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The charitable man beareth all injuries with patience.</ns0:note>, believeth all things <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">He believeth all things that are good of his brother, so far is he from being credulous to his prejudice.</ns0:note>, hopeth all things, endureth all things <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He endureth all things that a good man ought to endure, that is, any evils done to himself. In the same sense <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10.12. <ns0:hi>Love covereth all sins.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Charity never faileth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle, from another Argument, commendeth the <ns0:hi>Grace of Love, viz.</ns0:hi> its <ns0:hi>never <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ailing,</ns0:hi> it shall go with us into a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother World, and have its use and exercise there; where there will be no prophesying, no speaking with divers Tongues, but there the Saints shall love God. And this maketh it evident, that by <ns0:hi>Charity</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> (before mentioned) the Apostle doth not singly mean bounty or beneficence to those that stand in need of those good things of this life, in which we can help them.</ns0:note>: but whether <ns0:hi>there be</ns0:hi> prophecies, they shall fail; whether <ns0:hi>there be</ns0:hi> tongues, they shall cease <ns0:hi>b</ns0:hi>; whether <ns0:hi>there be</ns0:hi> knowledge, it shall vanish away <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Knowledge</ns0:hi> here, some understand the communi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cating of knowledge to the Church by preaching: others, the means we now have by meditating in, and study of the Scri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ptures: others better, of the imperfect degrees of our know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge, or the way of our procuring it; the following verses would incline us to interpret it of the former, though it be true also of the latter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 For we know in part <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It was truly said, as to things humane, That the greatest part of those things that we know, is the least part of those things which we are ignorant of. A great measure of Divine things is also unknown to us, and the knowledge of them reser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved for the Resurrection and Day of Judgment, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 14.20.</ns0:note>, and we prophesie in part <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Nor can the communication of our knowledge to that, be larger than what we by Prophecy communicate, we having our selves but a short and imperfect communication of Divine things, we can communicate but an imperfect degree of know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge to others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">But when we come to Heaven, we shall be in such a state, as nothing shall or can be added to us; then our partial and imperfect knowledge shall be swallowed up in a knowledge per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect and compleat.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Apostle compareth the state of Believers in this life, compared with their state in another life, to the state of a child, compared with that of a man. Look as one, when he is a child, knoweth things imperfectly, and discourseth of them in the stile, and according to the knowledge of a child: But when he is grown up, he discourseth of them at another rate, according to the degree of knowledge which he hath acquired by instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction of others, or his own experience and observation. So it is with all of us, in this life we, like children, have a poor, low, imperfect knowledge of spiritual things, and accordingly dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course of them: But when we come to Heaven, we shall know them, and discourse of them in a more perfect manner.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 3.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. & 5.7. Phil. 3.12.</ns0:note> now we see through a glass <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>in a rid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dle.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> darkly, but then <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Joh. 3.2.</ns0:note> face to face: now I know in part, but then shall I know, even as I am also known <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Apostle pursues his former Theme, comparing the imperfect state of Believers, as to knowledge in this life, with what shall be in the life that is to come.                <ns0:p n="13">13 And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three: but the greatest of these <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> charity <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Take us according to our state in this life, we have, and shall have the exercise of three Graces; <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> to evidence un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to us those things which we do not see, either by the eye of Sense or Reason: <ns0:hi>Hope,</ns0:hi> by which we wait for the receiving of them; and <ns0:hi>Love,</ns0:hi> by which we delight our selves in God, and shew obedience to the Will of God. But of all these, Love is the greatest, either in respect of its use and profitableness unto men, or in respect of its duration and abiding, (which last the Apostle seemeth chiefly to intend). <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> shall cease, when we come to the vision of God; and <ns0:hi>Hope,</ns0:hi> when we come to the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
